references_named: Jenny Holzer, Spectacolor LED board, Times Square (1982)
net.art (the scrolling-title trick / browser chrome as material)
rationale: The mechanism is the message: Holzer's anonymous authority-issuing truisms are relocated to document.title, the browser's one persistent public signage slot that follows the viewer across tab switches. The page itself is demoted to a footnote pointing back up at the tab, which is exactly the right inversion — the chrome is the gallery, the LED board, and the voice. The chance/order axis is legible (shuffled truisms driven by a strict character clock), the readymade logic is clean, and the double-coding lands: a funny tab editorialising at you on the surface, a precise Holzer critique underneath. Craft is restrained and complete: no storage, no network, CC BY-NC stated, attribution to Holzer and y-a-v-a, prefers-reduced-motion respected.
reservations: The 1990s scrolling-title gag is well-trodden net.art territory, so the novelty sits more in the precise Holzer framing than in the underlying trick. The catalogue already has several 'browser chrome as material' pieces (favicon-Mondrian, title-flip in Acid Action Painting, theme-color in Pure Colour), so the work's distinctiveness rests on the Holzer appropriation and the deliberate demotion of the page — which is genuinely fresh, but worth flagging.
revision_suggestion: Consider letting the truisms occasionally pause on a single line for a beat (a 'held' truism) before resuming the marquee, to mimic how Spectacolor boards actually dwell on statements — this would deepen the P5 tension and push the piece further from the generic scrolling-title trope.
